children: Confidence among U.S. home builders worsened in September as higher mortgage rates, labor shortages and rising costs weighed on builder sentiment.

The NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index, a gauge of builder confidence in the market for newly built single family housing fell three points to 32 in September. Economists polled by The Wall Street Journal expected a reading of 34.
"Buyer traffic has weakened across much of the country, largely because of rising mortgage rates," said NAHB Chairman Bill Owens.
As the conflict in Iran persists, Owens said builders also are continuing to face higher material costs, rising gas and diesel prices, and persistent labor shortages.

As the 10-year Treasury yield remains elevated, mortgage rates are closing in on 7% for the first time since the beginning of last year - a level that economists note could spook future buyers even further. The NAHB also said the index measuring current sales conditions fell four points to 35 this month.
In addition, 38% of builders cut prices in September, up from 35% in August, the survey found. The average price cut remained at 6% for the sixth consecutive month.
The index gauging future sales expectations dropped six points to 37 and the index charting prospective buyer traffic held steady at 23.
